```{r setup}
library(gamlssTools)
```

This vignette covers fitting gamlss models, as well as different diagnostic tools you can use to see if a model fits well 
and/or compare across different models/parameterizations.

Note that at the moment, much of this code works with the gamlss package only (not gamlss2). 

We'll use this toy dataset:

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
n <- 1000

# Age sampled uniformly on the log scale (birth = 280 days post-conception)
logAge <- runif(n, log10(196), log10(280 + 100 * 365.25))  # 28wk gestation to 100y
df <- data.frame(
  Age    = round(10^logAge - 280),   # days post-birth
  logAge = logAge,
  Sex    = factor(sample(c("Female", "Male"), n, replace = TRUE))
)

# Study assignment correlated with age
study_center <- c(Study_A = 2.55, Study_B = 3.15, Study_C = 3.70,
                  Study_D = 4.15, Study_E = 4.45)
study_width  <- 0.5                       # larger = more overlap between studies
study_size   <- c(1, 1, 0.8, 1.3, 0.6)     # relative recruitment volume

w <- outer(df$logAge, study_center, dnorm, sd = study_width)
w <- sweep(w, 2, study_size, "*")
df$Study <- factor(colnames(w)[apply(w, 1, function(p) sample.int(length(p), 1, prob = p))],
                   levels = names(study_center))

# Median trajectory (arbitrary volume-like units): fast perinatal rise,
# childhood peak, gradual decline through adulthood
growth  <- plogis((df$logAge - 2.70) / 0.22)
atrophy <- 1 - 0.38 * plogis((df$logAge - 3.85) / 0.32)
mu <- 900 * growth * atrophy

# Sex: males ~10% larger, with a small age interaction
mu <- mu * ifelse(df$Sex == "Male", 1.10 * (1 + 0.04 * (df$logAge - 3.5)), 1)

# Study/scanner offsets
mu <- mu * c(Study_A = 1.00, Study_B = 0.92, Study_C = 1.10,
             Study_D = 0.96, Study_E = 1.06)[df$Study]

# Multiplicative noise, wider in infancy -> heteroscedastic and right-skewed
sigma <- 0.05 + 0.07 * plogis(-(df$logAge - 3.0) / 0.35)
df$Pheno <- mu * exp(rnorm(n, 0, sigma))
```

# Model Fitting

Most model fitting can be done with the gamlss (or gamlss2) package functions. However, we add a couple of helpful wrappers.

First, `safe_gamlss()` broadcasts a couple of quiet "gotchas" you can run into when fitting gamlss models, namely quiet non-convergence
(i.e. returning something that looks like a gamlss model but in fact ran out of n.cyc before fitting), and some "Error" messages that are broadcast out as warnings.

Generally, you use `safe_gamlss()` exactly like you `gamlss()`

```{r}
#good fit model
pheno_model <- safe_gamlss(formula = Pheno ~ pb(logAge) + Sex + random(Study), 
                      sigma.formula= ~ pb(logAge) + Sex, data = df, family=BCCG)
```

```{r, error=TRUE}
#model that doesn't converge because very low n.cyc

#quiet gamlss warning
pheno_model_bad <- gamlss(formula = Pheno ~ pb(logAge) + Sex + random(Study), 
                      sigma.formula= ~ pb(logAge) + Sex, data = df, family=BCCG, n.cyc=2)

class(pheno_model_bad) #still looks like a gamlss model

#Loud safe_gamlss error
pheno_model_bad <- safe_gamlss(formula = Pheno ~ pb(logAge) + Sex + random(Study), 
                      sigma.formula= ~ pb(logAge) + Sex, data = df, family=BCCG, n.cyc=2)
```

The only downside is that using `summary()` on a model fit using `safe_gamlss()` returns a long, ugly `call` parameter.

It's very useful though as a sub-function to `gamlss_try()`, a wrapper function that enables you to easily run through
several gamlss modeling algorithms, adding more iterations, taking smaller steps, etc, to get your models to converge. 

It's also useful in that models which don't fit will return `NULL`, so you don't have to worry about missing a 
non-convergence warning OR about an error killing a whole HPC job or loop of model fits. This is useful for
things like model selection (which usually means fitting the same phenotype several ways, some of which may
not fit) or looping over many phenotypes to fit the same model on multiple outcomes.

The other reason to reach for `gamlss_try()` is that a fit which can't be rescued returns `NULL` rather than
stopping your script. Model selection usually means fitting the same phenotype several ways, and some of
those ways won't fit -- particularly in smaller samples. Here's a 60-subject pilot subsample, where BCPE
has more parameters than the data can support:

```{r, error=TRUE}
set.seed(9)
pilot <- df[sample(nrow(df), 60), ]

gamlss(formula = Pheno ~ pb(logAge) + Sex,
       sigma.formula = ~ pb(logAge),
       nu.formula = ~ pb(logAge),
       tau.formula = ~ pb(logAge),
       data = pilot, family = BCPE,
       control = gamlss.control(trace = FALSE))
```

That (very opaque) error would take down the loop or HCP job it was running in. `gamlss_try()` reports what it
tried, gives up, and returns `NULL`, so the rest of the candidate models still get fit:

```{r, message=TRUE}
base_args <- list(formula = Pheno ~ pb(logAge) + Sex,
                  sigma.formula = ~ pb(logAge),
                  nu.formula = ~ pb(logAge),
                  data = pilot,
                  control = gamlss.control(trace = FALSE))

candidates <- list(BCCG = list(family = BCCG),
                   BCT  = list(family = BCT,  tau.formula = ~ pb(logAge)),
                   BCPE = list(family = BCPE, tau.formula = ~ pb(logAge)))

pilot_models <- lapply(candidates, function(extra) do.call(gamlss_try, c(base_args, extra)))

sapply(pilot_models, is.null)
```

Then you can compare whichever models survived:

```{r}
fit_ok <- pilot_models[!sapply(pilot_models, is.null)]

sapply(fit_ok, `[[`, "sbc") #BIC
```

Here the BCCG model fits best! (See **Model Comparison** below)

# Model Diagnostics
Here "diagnostics" refer to making sure your model describes the data well.

The most helpful check is probably the worm plot. `wp.taki()` enhances the built-in `gamlss::wp()` by allowing you to break up plots along chunks of a continuous variable (like age) or by levels of a categorical variable (like sex), so you can make sure the model fits all groups well.

```{r}
#plot by age
wp.taki(xvar=df$logAge, resid=resid(pheno_model))

#plot by sex
df$Sex <- as.factor(df$Sex)
wp.taki(xvar=df$Sex, resid=resid(pheno_model))
```

Below is a quick illustrated reference for interpreting worm plots:
```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("wormplot_examples.jpg")
```

For more info, see:
Stasinopoulos, Dm & Rigby, Robert & Heller, Gillian & Voudouris, Vlasios & De Bastiani, Fernanda. (2017). Flexible regression and smoothing: Using GAMLSS in R. 10.1201/b21973. 

You can also check how well the predicted centiles for each point/subject line up with the percentiles themselves - that is, about 5% of subjects' centiles should be <= 0.05.

```{r}
centile_coverage(pheno_model, df)

#we can also view this by sex or age
centile_coverage(pheno_model, df, group="Sex")
centile_coverage(pheno_model, df, interval_var = "logAge", n=4)
```

Each of those calls re-scores every subject. If you've already calculated centiles (or scoring is
slow), hand them to `centile_coverage()` directly with the `centiles` argument instead of a model:

```{r}
df$centile <- score_centiles(pheno_model, df)

centile_coverage(data=df, centiles="centile", group="Sex")
```

# Model Comparison
It can be useful to compare two models fit on the same dependent variable. Often this is done for model selection (i.e. which parametrization fits best?). 

```{r}
#fit a new model with different splines
pheno_model2 <- gamlss(formula = Pheno ~ cs(logAge) + Sex + random(Study), 
                      sigma.formula= ~ cs(logAge) + Sex, data = df, family=BCCG)
```

First, we can return BIC and AIC built-into the gamlss model object

```{r}
#BIC
pheno_model$sbc < pheno_model2$sbc
#AIC
pheno_model$aic < pheno_model2$aic
```

Lower BIC (aka SBC) means a better fit model. We tend to use this over AIC.

It can also be useful to see how models compare in terms of the z-scores they assign the same dataset

```{r}
#compare z-scores
#note - need to supply the fit data for pheno_model2 since it contains cs()
compare_scores(pheno_model, pheno_model2, data=df, fit_data2 = df) 
```

Note that the function is set up to check for matching outputs, i.e. no differences between the two models. The default tolerance for "no" differences is 1e-6, or 1 millionth of y's standard deviation.

You can also use `compare_scores()` to check how the model's centile lines match up (i.e. compare the y-values of the estimated centile lines (as fit across each level of `sim_grid_list`) ...

```{r}
#compare centile lines
sim_list <- sim_grid(df, "logAge", "Sex")
compare_scores(pheno_model, pheno_model2, sim_grid_list = sim_list, fit_data2 = df) 
```

... though plotting them on top of one another is more intuitive

```{r}
compare_centile_fans(pheno_model, pheno_model2, df, "logAge", "Sex",
                      model_names=c("pb()", "cs()"),
                      show_points=TRUE,
                      get_peaks=TRUE,
                      sim_grid_list = sim_list) +
                      theme_bw()  
```

Whether you choose to do data-driven model selection (i.e. pick model with lowest BIC) or more qualitative selection (i.e. using fp() smooths
over pb() if the latter gives trajectories that are too wiggly to be biologically plausible) will depend on the goals of your project.
